claims.text: SLM-fabricated HEA components produced without active chamber preheating typically undergo rapid local cooling.
Rapid local cooling in conventionally fabricated SLM HEAs produces high thermal gradients and residual stresses.
Residual stresses in baseline SLM HEAs are associated with porosity and distortion.
Maintaining the SLM build chamber at 200–400 °C decreases the temperature difference between the molten pool and surrounding material.
Elevated chamber preheating reduces thermal gradients during solidification.
The reduced thermal gradient slows the cooling rate.
Reduced thermal gradients and slower cooling lessen residual-stress buildup.
Lower residual stress reduces distortion in SLM-fabricated HEA components.
Lower thermal shock from chamber preheating reduces the formation of pores and cracks.
Chamber preheating promotes a more uniform microstructure.
Chamber preheating promotes a refined microstructure.
A more homogeneous microstructure enhances the mechanical properties of SLM HEAs.
Preheated HEA components will have lower dimensional deviations, warping, and shrinkage than ambient-chamber controls.
Preheated HEA components will have lower pore and crack densities than ambient-chamber controls.
Preheated HEA components will have greater tensile strength than ambient-chamber controls.
Preheated HEA components will have greater ductility than ambient-chamber controls.
The preheating intervention is expected to be effective for moderately sized components typical of laboratory-scale SLM systems.
The optimal preheat temperature may vary for extremely large builds or HEAs with narrow processing windows.
Excessive preheating can cause undesired phase transformations or microstructural coarsening.
A controlled comparison will hold laser power, scan speed, layer thickness, powder feedstock, and atmosphere constant while varying chamber temperature.
